Llao Llao is a good place to discover the natural scenery of the Lake District at a leisurely walking pace. Bariloche's official tourism office lists the municipal park among the stops on the Circuito Chico route and recommends walks through its forests.

The park has woodland trails and paths leading to the shores of the lakes. Municipal information identifies López Bay, Villa Tacul and the Arrayanes forest among its natural attractions. The specific trail is chosen separately, taking into account access and walking conditions.

On the fishing trip with Lakeshore Chalet, a walk in the Llao Llao area is offered as an optional activity on a free day. It offers a change of scenery between outings to the Limay River; a visit to the park is not part of the tour's guaranteed main itinerary.

In northwestern Argentina, amid the arid valleys and imposing peaks of the Andes, Los Cardones National Park stretches across a remarkable landscape of giant cacti, rocky slopes and vast high-altitude plains. Situated primarily in Salta Province, the park is known for its striking contrasts and a sense of unspoiled stillness.

The most distinctive feature here is the cardón: a tall, column-shaped cactus rising from the ground like a natural sentinel of the desert. Some reach several metres in height, growing among rocks against a backdrop of ochre hills and distant mountain ranges. Their silhouettes give the scenery an almost otherworldly appearance, particularly at dawn and before sunset, when the sunlight turns the valleys shades of gold and copper-red.

The park encompasses several natural environments: dry valleys, mountain slopes, highland plateaus and patches of sparse vegetation adapted to the harsh climate. Unusual geological formations, broad open plains and winding mountain roads offer sweeping panoramas of the Andes. The famous Piedra del Molino Pass is especially scenic, with views over the Calchaquí Valley and the surrounding mountains.

Despite the demanding conditions, the park is home to a variety of Argentine wildlife. Guanacos, foxes, armadillos and many species of birds live here. Birds of prey can be spotted soaring on warm air currents above the open spaces, while animals well adapted to the dry environment shelter among the rocky vegetation.

Los Cardones is both a natural attraction and a place to experience the distinctive landscapes of northwestern Argentina. A visit often forms part of a journey through the Calchaquí Valleys, the wine-growing countryside around Cafayate and the colourful towns of Salta Province.

Los Cardones National Park captivates visitors with its rugged beauty and extraordinary sense of space. Nature is expressed here in simple forms and vivid colours, while the towering cacti against the Andes create one of northern Argentina's most memorable landscapes.

Los Flamencos National Reserve comprises several separate natural areas. They include Miscanti and Miñiques lagoons, the Chaxa area of the Atacama Salt Flat and the Valley of the Moon.

Each stop reveals a different landscape: volcanic highlands, shallow waters with flamingos or the dry rock formations of the Cordillera de la Sal. Exploring the reserve usually involves separate excursions from San Pedro de Atacama.

As the road crosses the highlands of Santa Cruz, the landscape becomes greener and more humid. Here lie Los Gemelos, or the Twin Craters: two large depressions on opposite sides of the road. They formed when rock collapsed over emptied magma chambers. From the rim, you can see the steep walls dropping away, while vegetation gradually conceals the dark volcanic rock.

Scalesia forest grows around the depressions. These native trees have an unusual botanical lineage: they belong to the same family as familiar daisies. The tree canopy, ferns and damp air make this place feel entirely different from the island's dry coast. It is a pleasure to follow a trail and look down over the forest, then take a closer look at the leaves and trunks nearby.

Los Gemelos also appeals to birdwatchers. Finches and other land birds of the Galápagos inhabit the green forest. The stop complements excursions out to sea, offering a glimpse of Santa Cruz's volcanic past and its living landscape today.
